title: Can You Get Dynamic Currency Conversion Fees Back After Signing the Receipt Abroad?
summary: At a nasi kandar counter in Penang, the cashier hands you the card terminal. The screen asks: USD or MYR? You tap USD because it looks familiar, then sign…
body_markdown:
At a nasi kandar counter in Penang, the cashier hands you the card terminal. The screen asks: USD or MYR? You tap USD because it looks familiar, then sign. Can you get that markup back later? Usually not. A signed dynamic currency conversion receipt is the merchant's evidence that you agreed, and card disputes turn on whether you agreed. You have a real case only when the conversion happened without your choice, for example when the currency was picked for you or no rate was shown. Moreta builds a wallet that pays local QR codes in local currency, with the exchange rate shown before you confirm.


**About the Author:**


This guide is written by the team at Moreta. Moreta is a Y Combinator-backed, FinCEN-registered Money Services Business whose app lets travelers pay local QR networks in local currency, including[DuitNow QR](https://moretapay.com/networks/duitnow) in Malaysia,[Pix](https://moretapay.com/networks/pix) in Brazil and[WeChat Pay](https://moretapay.com/networks/wechat-pay) in China.


## What is DCC, and why does signing the receipt matter?


Recovery is hard because of how DCC is built. Dynamic currency conversion is an option offered at a foreign card terminal or ATM. It converts your purchase into your home currency on the spot, using a rate set by the merchant's payment provider rather than your card network. Your issuer receives a charge already in dollars or pounds, so it never applies its own rate.


Signing a DCC receipt works like signing a courier's delivery note that says the parcel arrived intact. You can complain about the dent afterwards. But the first thing the courier will show is your signature. On many chip terminals, the "signature" is simply your tap on the home-currency button, and the terminal records that tap.


## Can you dispute a DCC charge after you signed?


Since consent decides everything, your odds depend on what actually happened at the terminal. Your issuer files the chargeback.


Swipe for more


What happened at the counter Realistic refund chance What to do


You noticed before leaving Good Ask the merchant to void it and re-run in local currency


Merchant chose the currency, no screen shown Reasonable Dispute it with your issuer as conversion without consent


Currency pre-selected, no rate disclosed Reasonable Dispute it, and note the missing disclosure


You saw both options and picked home currency Low Ask for goodwill. A chargeback will likely fail


The honest assessment: if you knowingly chose your home currency, treat the markup as tuition. Put your effort into the cases where nobody asked you.


## How do you file a DCC dispute with your card issuer?


If your case fits a "never asked" row above, speed and paperwork decide the outcome. Your issuer may set its own internal deadline, so contact it within days.


1. Photograph the receipt so both currencies and any printed rate are visible.


2. Write down who handled the terminal, whether you were shown a choice, and the time and place.


3. Call your issuer and use the phrase "dynamic currency conversion without consent."


4. Calculate what the local-currency amount should have cost at your network's rate that day, and claim the difference.


5. Reply quickly if the issuer asks for more after the merchant responds.


## What should you do when an ATM offers to convert?


The same consent logic applies at cash machines, where it is even easier to accept by accident. Search "decline conversion ATM" and you'll find the same advice everywhere, because it holds. When the screen offers to charge you in your home currency, decline and choose local currency. A conversion you accepted on an ATM screen is very hard to dispute, because the machine logged your button press. Read each screen slowly. The decline option sometimes appears as "without conversion" or as the local currency code alone.


## Does choosing the right travel card stop DCC?


A related question is whether a better card makes DCC go away. It doesn't. The merchant's side of the transaction offers DCC, so the prompt can appear for any Visa or Mastercard.


People spend evenings on Wise vs Revolut threads and "best travel card 2026" roundups. Comparing Wise vs Revolut fees or looking for cards without foreign transaction fees matters. But those numbers only apply if you pay in local currency. Accept DCC and your card's exchange rate is never used.


## How does paying by local QR code avoid the DCC question?


The cleanest way around the DCC prompt is to pay on a rail that never shows one. Merchants in Malaysia, Brazil and China take payment on local QR networks (DuitNow QR, Pix, WeChat Pay) that settle in ringgit, reais or yuan. That payment flow has no home-currency prompt at all.


With Moreta Pay, the steps are:


1. Top up from your home bank account or card in your own currency.


2. Scan the same code locals scan, such as the laminated DuitNow sign taped beside the till at a Bukit Bintang kopitiam.


3. Check the merchant name, amount and exact exchange rate before confirming.


4. Slide to pay. The merchant receives ringgit instantly.


If you're comparing options for the best currency exchange app, apply this test to every one: is the rate shown before you pay the rate actually used? Cash still has a place. A temple donation box in Penang or the attendant collecting coins outside a bus-terminal toilet will want notes. Keep a small cash reserve in local currency, withdrawn once with the conversion declined.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### **Can I get DCC fees refunded if I signed the receipt?**


Rarely. The signed receipt is evidence that you consented. A refund is realistic only if you ask the merchant to void it before you leave, or if you weren't offered a choice or the merchant picked the currency for you.


### **How long do I have to dispute a DCC charge?**


Deadlines vary by card network and issuer, so ask your issuer for its exact deadline. Call your issuer within days.


### **Is dynamic currency conversion illegal?**


No. It is legal when disclosed.


### **Should I pay in local currency or home currency abroad?**


Pay in local currency. Your card or wallet then applies its own rate instead of the merchant provider's rate.


### **Does a card without foreign transaction fees protect me from DCC?**


No. DCC is offered at the terminal, so you still have to decline it yourself.


### **Can a hotel reverse a DCC charge at checkout?**


It may, if you ask before leaving. A front desk that ran the charge may be able to void it and re-run it in local currency. Once you've left, your only route is a dispute.
